hops.title: Say it: leaves are the dirt's umbrella
hops.text: Try this as you lift the watering can over the grass tray: "Leaves are the dirt's umbrella. They catch fast raindrops before they smack the ground." Big trees do the same job. In one Forest Service study in Southern California, a medium-sized tree was estimated to catch about 2,380 gallons of rain a year, shielding the soil below.

sources.citation: Center for Urban Forest Research, Pacific Southwest Research Station, USDA Forest Service, Fact Sheet #4: Control Stormwater Runoff with Trees (2002).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Parent and child seen from behind in yellow raincoats looking up at a leafy tree in light rain.
image.caption: Leaves catch falling raindrops, so the drops reach the soil more gently.

hops.title: Ask it: what a raindrop feels like to dirt
hops.text: Ask your child, "If you were a tiny grain of dirt on bare ground, what would a big raindrop feel like?" Expect a splash, a wave or a water balloon! Laugh, then share that the biggest raindrops can fall at about 20 miles an hour, and when they hit bare dirt they can splash grains of it into the air.

sources.citation: Rain or Shine: An Introduction to Soil Physical Properties and Processes, 'Raindrop Impact', Oklahoma State University Libraries open textbook (same text also on LibreTexts Geosciences).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Close-up of a raindrop hitting bare soil and splashing tiny grains upward beside green grass blades.
image.caption: A big raindrop landing on bare dirt can splash grains of soil into the air.

hops.title: Point at it: pace out a tree's hidden roots
hops.text: On a park path away from roads, start under the outer edge of a big tree's branches and count big steps away from the trunk together. The roots may still be under your shoes. A tree's big roots usually grow in the top 18 inches of soil, and some trees' roots spread four times as wide as the branches above.

sources.citation: Emily Swihart, 'Where the tree roots grow', University of Illinois Extension, Good Growing blog (2026).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Parent and child seen from behind taking big steps along a park path away from a large oak tree.
image.caption: Some trees' roots spread four times as wide as their branches.

audio.title: Three playful ways to talk about roots and rain
audio.transcript:
Before you pick up the watering can, here are three easy ways to make this muddy little experiment stick.

First, while you pour onto the grass tray, try calling the leaves the dirt's umbrella. Kids get that picture right away. Big trees do the same job. In one Forest Service study in Southern California, a medium-sized tree was estimated to catch about two thousand three hundred eighty gallons of rain in a year. All those leaves help shield the soil below. Grass leaves do that for your tray, which is one reason the grass tray stays calmer than the bare one.

Second, ask your child a silly question: if you were a tiny grain of dirt on bare ground, what would a big raindrop feel like? You might hear a splash, a wave, or a water balloon. All good answers. Then share the real number. The biggest raindrops can fall at about twenty miles an hour, and when they land on bare dirt, they can splash grains of it right up into the air.

Finally, take the idea outside on your next park walk. Find a park path away from roads that passes under a big tree's outer branches, and count big steps together as you walk away from the trunk. Many people picture roots stopping right under the trunk, so this is a fun surprise: a tree's big roots usually grow in the top eighteen inches of soil, and some trees' roots spread four times as wide as the branches above. Your child may be standing right on top of them.

Keep it light, let your child guess first, and enjoy getting a little muddy together.
